652.title: The Sita who wasn't there
652.hook: Indrajit cuts Sita down in front of the army, or seems to: it's maya
652.carry: maya makes the false look real; look again
652.howItsDone: Some Ramayana tellers use the illusory Sita, the māyā-sītā of this episode, to talk about māyā, illusion, and how fear can make what is false look real.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Hanuman Chalisa, and how two herb flights became one picture on shrine walls. many tellings, one rama, kept alive by reciting.
screen: `MANY TELLINGS, ONE RAMA, KEPT ALIVE BY RECITING.`

segments.voice: Indrajit rides out of Lanka's western gate with a woman in his chariot. She's thin, in a soiled garment, weeping, calling Rama's name. Hanuman sees her and freezes. He sat in the tree above her in the ashoka grove; he knows that face. It's Sita. In front of the whole monkey army, Indrajit seizes her by the hair, draws his sword, and cuts her down. Then he shouts across the field: there's nothing left to fight for now.
screen: `A WOMAN IN THE CHARIOT.` → `HANUMAN FREEZES.` → `NOTHING LEFT TO FIGHT FOR.`

segments.voice: Hanuman, who crossed the sea to find her, pulls the army back in despair and goes to tell Rama. Rama, hearing it, collapses. Then Vibhishana arrives, the one person in the camp who knows how Lanka thinks. That wasn't Sita, he says. Ravana would never allow her to be killed; he wants her too much. It was an illusion, a magic double, and a distraction. Right now Indrajit is at Nikumbhila, a sacred grove and shrine, to complete a fire offering. If he finishes it, he'll be unbeatable. But Brahma's boon has a condition: whoever attacks him there, before the rite is done, can kill him. Tellers call that false woman maya-sita, the illusion Sita. And maya is one of Hinduism's big words. It means a power that makes things appear, and in Vedanta, one school of Hindu philosophy, it names the way the world can look like the whole truth when it isn't. Many teachers use this scene to show how maya works on us: it doesn't need to be real; it only needs to grip the heart. The tradition's answer has a name too: viveka, discernment, telling the real from the seeming. Notice that Vibhishana isn't stronger than anyone. He looks again, with a calm mind, and knows. Rama, steadied, sends Lakshmana off with Vibhishana, Hanuman and an army. The race to Nikumbhila begins.
screen: `RAMA COLLAPSES.` · `VIBHISHANA: IT WAS AN ILLUSION.` · `MAYA: WHAT APPEARS, NOT WHAT IS.` · `IT ONLY NEEDS TO GRIP THE HEART.` · then, large: `MAYA MAKES THE FALSE LOOK REAL. LOOK AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Picture a fear your mind has been showing you lately, a scene of something going wrong. Breathe slowly. If you pray, say Rama's name softly on each breath, the way many Hindus steady the mind with a name of God; if you don't, just say: look again. Then ask, in Vibhishana's calm voice, what you actually know. That's viveka, practiced small.
Indrajit's death. It begins with his cruelest trick, a magic Sita cut down before the army, and Vibhishana seeing through it to the fire at Nikumbhila.
Your line: maya makes the false look real; look again. The race reaches the grove next. Day six hundred fifty-two.

653.title: An arrow resting on truth
653.hook: an uncle and a nephew face each other at the fire, and Lakshmana makes a vow on his brother's name
653.howItsDone: Lakshmana's vow before the final arrow, resting on Rama's righteousness and truth, is often quoted by Ramayana teachers. Satyameva jayate, from the Mundaka Upanishad, is India's national motto, written beneath its state emblem.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Indrajit's cruelest trick, a magic Sita cut down to stop the army, and Vibhishana seeing through the maya. Maya makes the false look real; look again.

The grove at Nikumbhila is dark with trees, and somewhere inside, a fire is burning. Lakshmana's army crashes into the rakshasas guarding it, and the fighting gets so loud and close that Indrajit has to leave his offering unfinished and come out. He climbs into his chariot. And the first face he sees in the enemy line isn't Lakshmana's. It's his uncle's: Vibhishana, who knew about the fire, the grove and the secret condition, and brought them here.
screen: `THE FIRE IN THE GROVE.` → `THE RITE LEFT UNFINISHED.` → `HIS UNCLE'S FACE.`

segments.voice: Indrajit's words are bitter. You were born here, he says, you're my father's brother, and you've brought the enemy to your own nephew. Vibhishana answers without shouting. I was born among the rakshasas, but my nature isn't cruel. I left my brother because of what he was doing: carrying off another man's wife, harming those who had done him no wrong. Then the duel begins, Lakshmana and Indrajit, long and close: chariots wrecked, armor split, both men bleeding. At last Lakshmana fits the weapon of Indra, king of the gods, to his bow, and before he lets it go, he speaks a vow. If Rama, son of Dasharatha, is righteous, true to his word and unmatched in courage, then let this arrow kill Ravana's son. The arrow flies, and Indrajit falls. Lakshmana doesn't rest the arrow on his own strength. He rests it on his brother's truth. Scholars call this kind of vow an act of truth: if what I say is true, let it happen. Behind it sits one of Hinduism's oldest convictions: truth, satya, isn't only not lying. It's a power that holds the world up, and in the end it wins. The Mundaka Upanishad says it in three words: satyameva jayate, truth alone triumphs. India took them as its national motto. In Lanka, Ravana hears and loses his mind with grief. He rushes toward the ashoka grove to kill Sita. A minister named Suparshva steps in front of him. You, a learned king, would kill a woman? Fight Rama instead. Ravana turns back.
screen: `YOU BETRAYED YOUR FAMILY.` · `THE DUEL BEGINS.` · `A VOW ON RAMA'S TRUTH.` · `AN ACT OF TRUTH.` · then, large: `SATYAMEVA JAYATE. TRUTH ALONE WINS.` · `SUPARSHVA STOPS THE SWORD.`

If you don't, say: truth alone wins.

654.title: The vow of refuge
654.hook: a spear meant for Vibhishana, a brother who steps in front of it, and a chariot sent from heaven
654.carry: sharanagati: whoever comes for refuge is safe
654.howItsDone: Ramlila performances across North India build toward Ravana's final battle over many nights. Many follow Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas, where the wounding of Lakshmana that audiences know best comes earlier, from Meghnad (Indrajit), and Sushena and Hanuman's mountain save him there.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Indrajit's death at Nikumbhila, by Indra's own weapon, on a vow resting on Rama's truth. Satyameva jayate, truth alone wins.

Ravana has no one left to send. His brother Kumbhakarna is dead. His son Indrajit is dead. Most of his champions are gone. So he puts on his armor, mounts his great chariot, and rides out through the gates himself, with whatever army remains. The monkeys scatter before him. And in the enemy line he sees the brother who left him, Vibhishana. Ravana picks up a great spear, made to kill, and aims it at him.
screen: `NO ONE LEFT TO SEND.` → `RAVANA RIDES OUT.` → `A SPEAR AIMED AT VIBHISHANA.`

segments.voice: Lakshmana sees it, and doesn't hesitate. He fires at Ravana again and again, drawing his attention away from Vibhishana. Remember the shore, when Vibhishana came across the sea asking for refuge and the monkeys wanted him killed as a spy. Rama said: whoever comes to me even once, saying I am yours, I give safety from every being. That is my vow. Hindus call this sharanagati, taking refuge, and in some traditions, like the Sri Vaishnavas of South India, that verse is treasured as God's own promise to anyone who surrenders. Now Lakshmana keeps the vow with his body. Ravana turns the spear on him: you saved him, so take this instead. It strikes Lakshmana in the chest, and he falls. Rama pulls it out, breaks it, and weeps beside his brother. What would I do with victory without Lakshmana? Sushena, the monkey physician, says he isn't dead; his face hasn't changed. Once more Hanuman brings herbs from a mountain. Sushena holds one to Lakshmana's nose, and he breathes it in and gets up. Then Indra sends his own chariot down to Rama, who has fought this whole war on foot, with his charioteer, Matali, at the reins. Rama walks around it with respect and climbs aboard. Ravana in his chariot, Rama in Indra's. The last battle can begin.

655.title: The heart of the sun
655.hook: a sage with a hymn to the sun, heads that grow back, and one last arrow
655.carry: turn to the sun: the aditya hridayam
655.howItsDone: Devotees recite the Aditya Hridayam, especially at sunrise, and on Dussehra (Vijayadashami) Ramlila performances in North India end with Ravana's effigy being burned.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Lakshmana took a spear meant for Vibhishana, keeping Rama's vow of refuge, and Matali brought Indra's chariot down. Sharanagati: whoever comes for refuge is safe.

The duel has gone on so long that Rama is worn out. He stands in Indra's chariot, tired to the bone, with Ravana in front of him ready to fight again. And in that pause, Valmiki says, the sage Agastya, who had come with the gods to watch, walks up to Rama on the battlefield: the same sage who gave Rama weapons years ago in the forest. This time he doesn't bring a weapon. He brings a hymn.
screen: `WORN OUT.` → `AGASTYA WALKS UP.` → `NOT A WEAPON. A HYMN.`

segments.voice: It's called the Aditya Hridayam, the heart of the sun, a hymn praising the sun as the source of light and life. Agastya teaches it to Rama there and then, and tells him to recite it three times. Rama does, facing the sun, and Valmiki says his weariness lifts and his heart fills with courage. Hindus have honored the sun as a face of the divine since the Vedas: Surya, who gives light and life to everything. Many still greet it at dawn, some with this very hymn, some by pouring a little water toward it, an offering called arghya. Then the fight resumes, and it's terrifying. Rama cuts off one of Ravana's heads, and another grows in its place. Again and again, Valmiki says, a hundred times. Matali, the charioteer, reminds Rama of the weapon of Brahma, given to him long ago by Agastya. Rama takes it up. It blazes like the fire at the end of time. He charges it with the proper mantra, draws his bow to the full, and lets it go. The arrow strikes Ravana in the chest, and he falls from his chariot. The gods rain flowers. On Dussehra, also called Vijayadashami, towns in North India set giant effigies of Ravana alight to mark this victory. In the book, the moment is quieter: a tired man turns to the sun, and then one arrow.
screen: `THE HEART OF THE SUN.` · `SURYA: GIVER OF LIGHT AND LIFE.` · `ARGHYA: WATER FOR THE RISING SUN.` · `RAVANA FALLS.` · then, large: `A TIRED MAN TURNS TO THE SUN.`

656.title: Mandodari's lament
656.hook: Ravana's queen walks onto the battlefield, and says what no one else could say
656.carry: mastering the senses is never done once
656.howItsDone: Some Hindus recite a traditional verse naming five revered women of the epics, the pañcakanyā, with Mandodari among them, and some say it in the morning; versions differ on one of the names.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Aditya Hridayam. A tired Rama turned to the sun, and one arrow ended the war. Turn to the sun.

When the noise of victory dies down, the gates of Lanka open, and the women of Ravana's palace come out onto the battlefield. They've lost husbands, sons, brothers. They walk among the dead, weeping, until they find him. One of them comes forward and kneels by the body. She is Mandodari, Ravana's chief queen, Indrajit's mother. She has lost her son, and now her husband. Valmiki lets her speak over him at length.
screen: `THE GATES OPEN.` → `THE WOMEN COME OUT.` → `MANDODARI KNEELS.`

segments.voice: Her lament holds love and truth at the same time. She remembers who he was. You frightened the gods, she says; the earth and the mountains trembled at your name. How could a man on foot, wandering in the forest, bring you down? First she answers that Rama can't be only a man; he must be Vishnu himself, come in human form. A queen of Lanka says it out loud, over her husband's body. Then she names Ravana's own part, gently and without flinching. Long ago, she says, you conquered your senses, and with that discipline you conquered the three worlds. Now it's as if your senses remembered, and took their revenge. Your desire for Sita did what no army could. This is one of Hinduism's most repeated teachings. The Upanishads picture the senses, the indriyas, as strong horses pulling the chariot of the body, and the Bhagavad Gita warns that the restless senses can carry off the mind even of a wise person who is striving. Mastery isn't won once and kept. It's one reason many Hindus keep vrats, small fasts and vows, again and again: practice in holding the reins. Ravana's tapas was legendary, and he stopped holding them. Then Mandodari simply grieves: her husband, her son, her life in pieces. Later tradition honored her among the five women, the panchakanya, whose remembrance is said to wash away wrongdoing. She saw him whole, and mourned him anyway.

657.title: Enmity ends at death
657.hook: after Mandodari's grief, a funeral, a coronation, and two acts of mercy
657.howItsDone: Rama's words that enmity ends at death (maraṇāntāni vairāṇi) and Sita's mercy toward her guards are quoted by Hindu teachers on forgiveness and on treating the dead with respect.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Mandodari, kneeling by Ravana, naming the senses he once mastered, and how they took their revenge. Mastering the senses is never done once.
screen: `MASTERING THE SENSES IS NEVER DONE ONCE.`

segments.voice: Mandodari's lament ends. The other women lift her gently and lead her back toward the city. Ravana's body still lies on the field. Someone has to perform his funeral rites, and by custom that duty falls to his closest kin: Vibhishana. But Vibhishana stands back. He tells Rama he can't do it. This man was cruel, he says, he wronged others' wives, he was against everything right. How can I honor him?
screen: `MANDODARI LED HOME.` → `A KING STILL ON THE FIELD.` → `VIBHISHANA STANDS BACK.`

segments.voice: Rama's answer is short, and it is still quoted. Enmity ends at death. Our purpose is finished. Perform his rites. He is mine now, as much as he is yours. Think about who's saying this: the man whose wife Ravana stole, whose brother Ravana nearly killed. The moment the war is over, Rama refuses to carry the hatred one step further. Ravana was a great warrior, he says, and deserves a king's funeral. So Vibhishana does it, with fire and ritual, as a brother. These last rites, antyeshti, are the final rite of passage of a Hindu life, and Rama won't let even his enemy be denied them. Mandodari saw Ravana whole; Rama lets him be honored whole. Then Rama has Vibhishana crowned king of Lanka, properly this time, and sends Hanuman into the city with the news for Sita. There a second mercy waits. Hanuman finds Sita in the grove, surrounded by the rakshasi guards who threatened her for months. He tells her Ravana is dead, and she's too moved to speak. Then he offers, angrily, to kill every one of the guards. Sita stops him. They were servants following a king's orders, she says. And then, in Valmiki, she says something that sounds like a whole teaching. A noble person shows compassion to the guilty and the good alike, because no one is without fault. Two people with every reason for revenge, Rama and Sita, on the same day, both refuse it.

658.title: Rama's hard words
658.hook: the reunion everyone has waited for, and the hardest words in the epic
658.carry: raja dharma, and the freedom to question it
658.howItsDone: Hindu teachers, scholars and storytellers discuss this scene from many sides, and some retellings, including women's songs and regional Ramayanas, give Sita's side of it at length.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Rama's words, enmity ends at death, Ravana's funeral rites, and Sita sparing the guards who tormented her.

For months, everything in this story has pointed to one moment. The search parties, the leap, the ring, the jewel, the bridge, the war. Now Vibhishana brings Sita out of the grove, bathed and dressed in fine clothes, carried toward Rama through a crowd of monkeys and rakshasas pressing to see her. Rama says: let her walk, so everyone can see. She steps down and walks toward him, shy and full of joy, looking at his face. What happens next has troubled readers, inside the tradition and out.
screen: `EVERYTHING POINTED HERE.` → `SITA WALKS TOWARD HIM.` → `WHAT HAPPENS NEXT.`

segments.voice: Rama does not take her in his arms. In Valmiki he speaks coldly, in front of everyone. I've won you back, he says, and wiped out the insult to my family's name. But know this: I didn't fight this war for you. I fought it for my honor. Then come the words that hurt most. She lived in another man's house for a long time, and he doesn't feel he can take her back. She's free to go wherever she likes. Valmiki doesn't soften it. Sita weeps, ashamed in front of the crowd, and those watching are shaken too. Hindus call Rama maryada purushottam, the best of men, who keeps every bound of duty. So how can he speak like this? Many teachers read the scene through raja dharma, a king's duty: a king must be seen to be beyond suspicion, so Rama speaks as a king, not a husband, putting his people's trust above his own heart. Some read it as a test meant for the world, not for Sita. Other readers, Hindu and not, find it simply wrong and side with Sita, and women's songs and regional Ramayanas give her side at length. Here's the teaching under all of it: dharma is subtle, and Hinduism doesn't ask you to stop thinking when you open its holiest stories. The tradition argues about dharma out loud, even Rama's. Tomorrow, Sita answers.
screen: `HE DOES NOT EMBRACE HER.` · `NOT FOR YOU, BUT FOR MY HONOR.` · `SITA WEEPS.` · `RAJA DHARMA: A KING'S DUTY.` · `READERS STILL ARGUE.` · then, large: `DHARMA IS SUBTLE. YOU MAY ASK.`

segments.voice: Hindus have long argued over their stories out loud: in families, in satsang, in the commentaries. Today, try it. Think of one part of this story, or of your own tradition, that troubles you. Breathe slowly, and say the question plainly, aloud or on paper, without rushing to an answer. If you pray, bring it to God as it is; the tradition lets Sita speak, and you can too. If you don't, simply hold the question with respect. Asking honestly is part of the practice.
